hints: Integrate by parts first with $u=x^2$ and $dv=\sin2x\,dx$.
Apply integration by parts again to the remaining $\int x\cos2x\,dx$.
Combine the terms into one antiderivative before substituting $0$ and $\pi/2$.
Use the exact sine and cosine values at both limits and simplify without decimals.
walkthrough:
Apply integration by parts $\int u\,\mathrm{d}v = uv - \int v\,\mathrm{d}u$ with:
$$u = x^2 \implies \mathrm{d}u = 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$$
$$\mathrm{d}v = \sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x \implies v = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x$$

Substitute into the integration by parts formula:
$$\int x^2\sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\cos 2x - \int \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right)(2x)\,\mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\cos 2x + \int x\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Apply integration by parts a second time to $\int x\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x$ with $u_1 = x \implies \mathrm{d}u_1 = \mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}v_1 = \cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x \implies v_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x$:
$$\int x\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x - \int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x$$

Combine to obtain the complete antiderivative:
$$\int_0^{\pi/2} x^2\sin 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = \left[-\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\cos 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x\right]_0^{\pi/2}$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\left(\dfrac{\pi^2}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{8} - \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{8} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}(\pi^2 - 4)$$
